title: Effect of Synthesis Parameters for Synthesizing Mesoporous ZnO Microparticles
content: Zinc oxide is regarded as non-toxic to living organisms. It is a widely researched transparent semiconductor with a wide band gap (Eg = 3.37 eV) and a high exciton binding energy (∼60 meV), offering promising applications in solar cells, antibacterial techniques, sensing, photocatalysis, and optical applications [1-5]. There are several methods to achieve this type of material. However, in many cases, they are complicated and expensive. On the other hand, mesoporous materials are highly versatile, and they have several applications in our lives due to their crystalline structure and physicochemical properties. They have high surface area which makes it an ideal material for energy absorption, catalysis and storage. Also, the mesopores can be structurally ordered, especially in materials such as mesoporous silica (MCM-41, SBA-15) and their permeability facilitates the transport of larger molecules, making it very useful for chemical and biological applications [1, 6]. Actually, there is few information about preparation of ZnO mesoporous microparticles. In this research work, both the synthesis of zinc oxide mesopores and the synthesis conditions that affect their pore size and surface area are presented. This research presents a simple and easy method for synthesizing mesoporous zinc oxide without using an organic template. The preparation of mesoporous zinc oxide samples was following, first, a solution (S1) was prepared by dissolving 0.02 mol of zinc acetate dihydrate (Sigma-Aldrich) in 21.6 g of distilled water. A second solution (S2) was prepared by dissolving 0.5 mol of NaOH (J.T. Baker) in 21.6 g of distilled water. Then, solution S2 was added to solution S1 slowly, drop by drop, and left stirring at 500 rpm for 30 min. The resulting gel was placed in a stainless-steel autoclave at 120 °C for one day in an oven to give hydrothermal treatment to the sample. Subsequently, the resulting suspension was washed with 100 ml of distilled water and centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 10 min. Then, the material obtained was dried in an oven at 80 °C for one day. Finally, the samples were calcined at 560 °C (with a ramp of 10°C/min) for 1 hour.
